title: Burnham Elevates Three Indian-Origin MPs in UK Cabinet Reshuffle
excerpt: Bihar-born Kanishka Narayan becomes UK's first dedicated AI minister at Cabinet level as new PM reshapes government with fresh 2024-intake talent, while veterans Seema Malhotra and Preet Kaur Gill return to the backbenches.
body:
• Kanishka Narayan, born in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, was elevated to Minister for Artificial Intelligence with a seat at the Cabinet table — the UK's first dedicated AI ministerial role at that level
  • Satvir Kaur and Harpreet Uppal, both first elected in 2024, were appointed to government roles as part of Burnham's wider ministerial appointments
  • Veteran Indian-origin MPs Seema Malhotra and Preet Kaur Gill lost their front-bench positions and returned to the backbenches after Burnham's purge of Starmer loyalists
  • The reshuffle saw 15 ministers dismissed from the previous cabinet — the largest clearout in a same-party transition since Boris Johnson's first government

Andy Burnham's sweeping cabinet reshuffle has given a prominent boost to a new generation of Indian-origin lawmakers, elevating three Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) from the 2024 parliamentary intake to government roles — even as two veteran PIO MPs were sent to the backbenches.

Narayan's Rise: From Bihar to the Cabinet Table

The most striking promotion went to Kanishka Narayan, the 36-year-old MP for Vale of Glamorgan who was born in Muzaffarpur, Bihar. Burnham elevated Narayan from his previous role as Parliamentary Under-Secretary for AI and Online Safety to a newly created Minister for Artificial Intelligence post that carries a seat at the Cabinet table — a first in British political history.

Narayan will serve jointly across the Cabinet Office and the newly expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, overseeing AI regulation, semiconductor investments and technology infrastructure. His appointment came after Burnham dissolved the standalone Department for Science, Innovation and Technology created by former PM Rishi Sunak in 2023, folding its functions into other departments.

"My relationship with India, both personally and professionally, remains a deep one and certainly a very regular one."

— Kanishka Narayan, MP for Vale of Glamorgan

Narayan's trajectory from Bihar to Westminster has been remarkable. His family moved to Cardiff when he was 12, and he grew up sleeping on the floor of a one-bedroom home off City Road. A scholarship took him to Eton College, followed by PPE at Balliol College, Oxford, and an MBA from Stanford University. He served as a civil servant in the Cabinet Office under David Cameron before winning his Welsh seat in July 2024, making history as the first ethnic-minority MP elected from Wales.

Satvir Kaur and Harpreet Uppal Join Government

Satvir Kaur, the MP for Southampton Test, was appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State at the Home Office and Minister for Equalities on July 22 — directly replacing Seema Malhotra in the equalities brief. Kaur, who was first elected in 2024, had previously served as Parliamentary Secretary in the Cabinet Office under Starmer. She made history in 2022 as the first female Sikh leader of a local authority in Britain when she led Southampton City Council.

Harpreet Uppal, the Sikh MP for Huddersfield, was appointed as an Assistant Government Whip. Uppal has a personal connection to Burnham — she worked on his 2017 campaign for Mayor of Greater Manchester, and he later endorsed her parliamentary candidacy. First elected in 2024, she had briefly served as Parliamentary Private Secretary to then-Deputy PM Angela Rayner before that role ended in September 2025.

Malhotra and Gill Lose Front-Bench Roles

The gains for the 2024 intake came at the expense of established Indian-origin parliamentarians. Seema Malhotra, the veteran Labour MP for Feltham and Heston who has held the seat since 2011, lost her dual role as Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Indo-Pacific at the Foreign Office and Minister for Equalities — positions she had held since September 2025.

Preet Kaur Gill, the MP for Birmingham Edgbaston and the first British Sikh woman elected to Parliament in 2017, also lost her position. She had been serving as Parliamentary Private Secretary to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology under Starmer, but was not reappointed by Burnham.

Both Malhotra and Gill had signed the unity letter backing Starmer during the Labour leadership crisis in May 2026, when 111 MPs rallied behind the then-PM as Burnham's challenge gathered momentum. Their removal fits a pattern across the reshuffle: Burnham dismissed 15 ministers from the previous cabinet, rewarding allies while clearing out Starmer loyalists, according to The Times.

Broader Diaspora Presence in the Burnham Cabinet

Despite the changes, Indian-origin representation at the senior cabinet level remains intact. Shabana Mahmood continues as Home Secretary, one of the most powerful positions in government. Lisa Nandy, whose father Dipak Nandy was a Kolkata-born academic, was retained as Culture Secretary — a post she has held since Labour came to power in July 2024.

Uma Kumaran, the MP for Stratford and Bow who is of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, was also appointed as Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Indo-Pacific, taking over the brief Malhotra had held. She simultaneously serves as an Assistant Government Whip.

The Times reported that Burnham's cabinet is the first in history with a majority of female ministerial appointments, with 12 of 23 cabinet members being women. Two of the ministers — Narayan and energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh — were born outside Britain, according to the newspaper's analysis.

What's Next

Narayan's elevation signals that AI policy will be a central pillar of Burnham's government. His appointment places Britain alongside the UAE, Canada and France, which have dedicated ministerial-level AI roles. For the Indian diaspora in the UK, the reshuffle represents a generational shift — from the steady presence of veterans like Malhotra and Gill to a younger cohort that entered Parliament just two years ago and is already shaping government policy at the highest levels.

Burnham, who took office on July 20, faces significant challenges: a sluggish economy, elevated borrowing costs, the ongoing US-Iran conflict affecting energy prices, and the rising electoral threat from Nigel Farage's Reform UK. Whether his bet on fresh talent — including the new Indian-origin appointees — delivers results will be tested quickly as Parliament returns for its first session under the new PM.
nri_angle: Three Indian-origin MPs from the 2024 intake were elevated to front-bench roles in Burnham's government, signaling a generational shift in British Indian political representation, while two veterans who had backed Starmer were dropped.
author: Diaspora Desk
